title: Architecture for Multi-Channel Service Delivery
objectives: Design architectures that support web, mobile, phone and face-to-face channels
Apply the GOV.UK channel strategy principles
Ensure consistency across channels without duplication of business logic
Support assisted digital and offline-first design patterns
Design for the GOV.UK app and future mobile channels
whyThisMatters:
Most government services are not purely digital. Citizens interact through web browsers, mobile devices, phone calls, face-to-face appointments, and posted letters. A parent claiming child benefit might start online, call HMRC when they get stuck, and receive a confirmation letter in the post. A business applying for a licence might begin on a desktop, continue on their phone, and attend an in-person interview.

The Government Digital Inclusion Strategy acknowledges that not everyone can or will use digital channels. Approximately 10% of UK adults have very low or no digital skills. Many more have situational barriers — unreliable connectivity, shared devices, or accessibility needs that are poorly served by a specific channel. The Service Standard (point 4: make the service simple to use) and the Digital Inclusion Action Plan require services to work across channels, not just the cheapest one.

For architects, multi-channel delivery is an architecture challenge, not just a UX challenge. If business logic is embedded in the web frontend, how does the contact centre agent apply the same rules? If eligibility checks are hardcoded into one channel, what happens when a new channel is needed? The architecture must separate what the service does (business logic, rules, decisions) from how users interact with it (channel-specific presentation and interaction patterns). Get this wrong and you end up maintaining parallel implementations of the same rules across channels — with inevitable inconsistencies that confuse users and create operational risk.

content.heading: The GOV.UK Channel Strategy and What It Means for Architects
content.body:
The UK government's approach to channels is guided by the principle of 'digital by default, but not digital only.' The Digital Strategy commits to making digital services so good that most people choose to use them — while ensuring alternatives exist for those who cannot.

This creates an architectural imperative: the digital channel should not be a privileged path with special access to business logic. Instead, all channels should access the same underlying service capability through well-defined interfaces. The digital channel may be the most efficient and the primary design focus, but it must not be the only path through the service.

Channel types in government services:

Web (desktop and mobile browser): the primary self-service channel. Citizens complete transactions independently. Accounts for 80-95% of transactions in mature digital services. Must meet WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility requirements.

GOV.UK app: the emerging mobile-native channel. Launched in 2024, it provides push notifications, document wallet, and quick access to personalised government information. Services can integrate via APIs to surface information and actions within the app. The app handles its own authentication via GOV.UK One Login.

Telephone: contact centres handle citizens who cannot use digital channels, who are stuck in a process, or who have complex situations. Agents need access to the same service functionality as the digital channel — but optimised for conversation-guided interaction rather than self-service forms.

Face-to-face: Jobcentre Plus offices, DVLA local offices, and appointment-based services where in-person interaction is necessary (identity verification, complex assessments, vulnerable users needing support).

Postal: some services still accept paper applications and send paper correspondence. Letter generation must use the same business rules and templates as digital notifications.

Third-party and intermediary: accountants submitting tax returns, solicitors filing company changes, charities applying on behalf of beneficiaries. These intermediaries need bulk or API access to service functionality.

The architectural principle: all these channels should be thin presentation layers over a shared service core. No business logic should live in a channel layer.

content.heading: Channel-Agnostic Service Layers and the BFF Pattern
content.body:
The fundamental architecture pattern for multi-channel services separates the service into layers:

The Domain Layer contains all business logic: eligibility rules, validation, workflow state machines, decision logic, and calculations. This layer knows nothing about channels. It exposes its capabilities through APIs that any channel can consume. When policy changes (for example, eligibility thresholds change), you update this layer once and all channels automatically reflect the change.

The Channel Layer (or BFF — Backend for Frontend) is specific to each channel. It handles: channel-specific authentication (GOV.UK One Login for citizens, departmental SSO for agents, mTLS for API consumers), interaction patterns (multi-page form journey for web, conversation flow for telephony, batch upload for intermediaries), data shaping (the web form needs specific field groupings, the agent screen needs a different layout, the API returns raw data), and channel-specific caching and performance optimisation.

The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern creates one BFF per channel type:

Citizen Web BFF: orchestrates the multi-page form journey, manages session state, handles save-and-return, validates input progressively, and shapes responses for the GDS Design System components.

Agent/Contact Centre BFF: provides a searchable view of citizen records, exposes the same transaction capabilities but with agent-specific workflows (record reason for call, note assisted digital usage, override validation for exceptional cases), and includes conversation scripting support.

Mobile/App BFF: returns minimal payloads optimised for mobile bandwidth, supports push notification registration, handles offline-capable data synchronisation, and respects device-specific constraints.

API BFF: provides RESTful or event-driven interfaces for third-party consumers, handles API key management and rate limiting, returns full payloads without channel-specific shaping, and supports bulk operations.

The key discipline: BFFs must not contain business logic. They orchestrate calls to the domain layer and shape responses for their channel. If you find eligibility rules or decision logic in a BFF, it has leaked from the domain layer and will diverge between channels.

content.heading: Offline-First and Progressive Enhancement
content.body:
Not all users have reliable connectivity. Rural areas, underground transport, mobile dead spots, and congested public Wi-Fi all create scenarios where government services must work with intermittent or no connectivity. The Digital Inclusion Action Plan recognises connectivity as a barrier alongside digital skills.

Offline-first architecture assumes connectivity is unreliable and designs for it:

Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) enable web services to function offline using service workers that cache application code and essential data locally. When connectivity returns, queued actions synchronise with the server. For government services, this means: form data saved locally until submission is possible, reference data (postcodes, drop-down options) cached for offline use, and clear indication to the user of what requires connectivity and what does not.

Conflict resolution becomes critical when offline-capable services synchronise. If a caseworker updates a record offline and another caseworker updates the same record online, the service needs a strategy: last-write-wins (simple but risks data loss), merge (complex but preserves both changes), or manual resolution (flag conflicts for human decision).

Graceful degradation ensures that when connectivity is limited, the service still provides value. A service might: allow form completion offline but queue submission until connectivity returns, show cached versions of reference data with a 'last updated' indicator, queue notifications for dispatch when connectivity permits, and provide clear feedback about what is available offline versus what requires connection.

For the GOV.UK app, offline capability is particularly important because mobile users frequently move between connected and disconnected states. The app architecture supports local storage of documents and status information, with background synchronisation when connectivity is available.

Architectural implications: offline-first requires careful thought about data ownership and authority. The server is authoritative for shared state (another user's actions), but the local device is authoritative for the current user's uncommitted work. Synchronisation protocols must handle this cleanly, and the user must always understand whether they are seeing live or cached information.

content.heading: Contact Centre Integration and Assisted Digital
content.body:
Approximately 30-40% of government service interactions still happen via telephone. Even for mature digital services, contact centres handle complex cases, vulnerable users, those who are stuck in a process, and those who simply prefer speaking to a human. Architecture must treat the contact centre as a first-class channel, not an afterthought.

Assisted digital is the government's term for supporting users who cannot complete digital transactions independently. This might mean: a contact centre agent completing the transaction on behalf of the citizen while on the phone, a face-to-face advisor guiding the citizen through the digital service on a shared screen, or a third party (family member, carer, charity worker) acting on the citizen's behalf.

Architectural patterns for contact centre integration:

Agent Desktop Integration: the contact centre BFF provides agents with a purpose-built interface that exposes the same service capabilities as the citizen channel but with additional features — citizen record search, transaction history, ability to start/resume/complete transactions on behalf of the citizen, and notes for recording the interaction.

Screen Pop: when a citizen calls, their phone number or reference number identifies them, and the agent's screen automatically displays their record and recent interactions. This requires integration between the telephony platform (often a cloud contact centre like Amazon Connect or Genesys) and the service's citizen record API.

Warm Transfer Context: when a call is transferred between agents or departments, the context of the conversation (what has been discussed, what the citizen needs) must transfer too. This requires a shared session or case model that is not tied to a specific agent.

Dual-Running: during assisted digital interactions, the agent may be completing the same journey as the citizen would online, but with the ability to bypass certain steps (e.g., skip the 'check your answers' page because the citizen has verbally confirmed) or add information (e.g., 'reason for phone contact: citizen unable to upload document').

Architectural consideration: the agent channel often needs elevated privileges — agents can search for citizens, view multiple records, override soft validations, and access restricted functions. This must be handled through role-based access control in the domain layer, not by giving the agent BFF direct database access. The domain layer enforces what agents can do; the BFF merely presents the interface.

content.heading: Letter Generation and the Postal Channel
content.body:
Despite digitisation, government still sends millions of letters. Benefit decisions, tax notifications, licence confirmations, and penalty notices all have legal or policy requirements for written correspondence. Letters are not going away — they are a channel that must be architecturally integrated.

Letter generation architecture:

Template Management: letters are defined as templates with merge fields populated from service data. Templates must be version-controlled (when the wording changes, in-flight letters use the version that was current when they were triggered), approved through content design governance (letters go through GDS content standards like any other content), and support Welsh language variants where required.

Generation Pipeline: when a service event triggers a letter (decision made, deadline approaching, reminder due), the notification service generates the letter content by merging the template with case data, formats it for print (PDF/A or print-ready format), and dispatches it to the print-and-post provider via their batch API.

Consistency with Digital Notifications: a citizen might receive an email via GOV.UK Notify AND a letter about the same event. The content must be consistent — same decision, same amounts, same deadlines. This means: one notification event triggers both channels, using shared data but channel-appropriate templates (letters are formal, emails can be more concise).

Tracking and Audit: unlike email (where delivery confirmation is available), letter delivery cannot be confirmed. The service records: when the letter was generated, when it was dispatched to the print provider, the print provider's batch reference, and the expected delivery window. Royal Mail tracking is available for recorded delivery items.

Return mail handling: letters returned as undeliverable (gone away, address unknown) must trigger a process — typically flagging the citizen's address as potentially invalid and triggering an address verification workflow.

Architectural principle: letters are just another notification channel. The same event-driven notification architecture that sends emails and SMS should also trigger letters. The template engine, merge data, and dispatch logic differ per channel, but the triggering events and business rules are shared. Do not build a separate 'letters system' disconnected from your notification architecture.

workedExample.title: Designing Multi-Channel Architecture for a DESNZ Energy Grants Service
workedExample.context: DESNZ is launching an energy efficiency grants service for homeowners. Research shows the user base is diverse: 60% are digitally confident homeowners who will self-serve online, 25% are older homeowners who prefer telephone assistance, 10% will use the service through energy advisors who visit homes and complete applications face-to-face, and 5% need paper applications. The service must: verify property eligibility (via EPC register), calculate grant amounts, process applications, manage caseworker assessments, disburse payments, and send notifications. All channels must deliver consistent outcomes — a citizen should get the same grant decision regardless of how they apply.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect designs a channel-agnostic architecture ensuring business rule consistency across all channels.

Domain Layer Design:
- Eligibility Service: takes property reference, checks EPC register, returns eligibility result and applicable grant amounts. No channel awareness.
- Application Service: accepts application data (property, applicant, measures requested), validates, creates application record. Same validation rules regardless of source.
- Assessment Service: manages caseworker workflow, records decisions. Shared across all channels.
- Payment Service: integrates with GOV.UK Pay for online or bank transfer for paper applications.
- Notification Service: sends confirmations, updates, and decisions via appropriate channel (email, SMS, or letter based on citizen preference and application channel).

Channel BFF Design:

Citizen Web BFF:
- Multi-page form journey following GDS patterns
- Progressive enhancement — core journey works without JavaScript
- Save-and-return using GOV.UK One Login
- EPC lookup integrated into the form flow
- Estimated: handles 60% of applications

Contact Centre BFF:
- Agent searches by property address, postcode, or applicant name
- Agent walks citizen through eligibility check verbally, enters data into agent form
- 'Complete on behalf of' workflow with mandatory 'reason for assisted application' field
- Script prompts guide agents through required questions
- Call recording reference linked to application for audit
- Estimated: handles 25% of applications

Energy Advisor BFF (tablet-optimised):
- Offline-capable: advisors download property data before home visits
- Form designed for tablet interaction during home visit
- Photo upload for property evidence (offline-queued)
- Synchronises completed applications when advisor returns to connectivity
- Advisor authentication via advisor portal credentials
- Estimated: handles 10% of applications

Paper Channel:
- PDF application form generated from same data model as digital form
- Paper applications scanned and entered by processing team using a data entry BFF
- Optical character recognition assists but human verification required
- Paper applications enter the same workflow as digital once digitised
- Estimated: handles 5% of applications

Cross-Channel Consistency:
- Eligibility rules live only in the Eligibility Service — no channel duplicates them
- Grant calculation lives only in the Application Service — consistent amounts regardless of channel
- All channels write to the same application data store — a caseworker sees all applications regardless of origin channel
- Notifications sent via citizen's stated preference, not via the application channel (a phone applicant might prefer email updates)
workedExample.outcome: The service launches with web and telephone channels first (covering 85% of users), adds the advisor channel in the second release, and paper applications in the third. Business logic changes (e.g., updated grant amounts following policy changes) are made once in the domain layer and immediately apply to all channels. A service assessment finds no inconsistencies between channels — the same eligibility check produces the same result regardless of channel. Contact centre agents report that the purpose-built agent interface is faster than the previous approach of navigating the citizen website on behalf of callers.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The critical design decision was placing all business logic in the domain layer with strict enforcement that BFFs contain no rules or calculations. This required discipline during development — developers were tempted to add 'just this one validation' in the BFF for speed. The architect established a simple test: if a rule change would require updating more than one BFF, the rule is in the wrong place. The offline-capable advisor channel required the most architectural thought but served a vital user need — energy advisors visiting homes in rural areas often had no mobile signal.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Desktop-Only Service That Failed Mobile and Phone Users
civilServiceScenario.background: A department launched a digital service for citizens to report changes in circumstances affecting their benefit entitlement. The service was designed and tested primarily on desktop browsers. Six months after launch, analytics reveal: 55% of users attempt the service on mobile devices, but only 30% of mobile users complete the transaction (vs 78% on desktop). The contact centre reports a 300% increase in calls from citizens saying 'I tried to do it online but it did not work on my phone.' The service has no contact centre integration — agents must ask citizens to 'try again on a computer' or manually process the change using a separate internal system with different business rules, leading to inconsistent outcomes. Paper forms exist but use an outdated version of the eligibility rules. The service fails its live assessment because it does not meet the Service Standard requirement to work for everyone who needs it.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: Redesign the architecture to properly support mobile users, enable contact centre agents to complete transactions on behalf of citizens, and ensure consistency across all channels.
constraints: 55% of users are on mobile devices — mobile is the primary channel, not secondary
The current frontend embeds business logic in JavaScript — eligibility calculations happen client-side
The contact centre uses a separate legacy system with different (outdated) business rules
The paper form references eligibility criteria from 18 months ago
Budget allows incremental improvement over 3 sprints, not a full rewrite
The service processes 2,000 changes per week
Citizens receive different outcomes depending on which channel they use (a compliance risk)
The Service Standard assessment failed on points 4 (simple to use) and 5 (make sure everyone can use the service)
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect brought in to fix the multi-channel failures.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
The root cause is an architecture that treated 'the website' as 'the service.' Business logic embedded in client-side JavaScript means the service only works properly in the specific browser environments where it was tested. The contact centre running a separate system means outcomes diverge between channels — a genuine compliance risk if citizens receive different benefit decisions depending on how they report changes.

The incremental fix over 3 sprints:

Sprint 1: Extract business logic from the frontend into a server-side API. The web frontend becomes a thin client that calls the API for eligibility checks and calculations. This immediately fixes mobile issues because the logic runs server-side regardless of device. The responsive CSS issues are fixed in parallel.

Sprint 2: Build a contact centre BFF that calls the same domain API. Agents can now complete transactions with identical business rules to the digital channel. Retire the legacy system for this service's transactions.

Sprint 3: Update paper forms to reflect current rules, build a data-entry interface for processing paper applications that also calls the domain API, and implement a notification service that confirms changes regardless of the submission channel.

The key architectural principle established: the API is the service. Channels are presentation layers over it. No business logic exists outside the API. This principle prevents the same problem recurring as new channels are added.

practiceArtefact.description: Design a multi-channel architecture for a government service that allows citizens to renew driving licences. The service must support: web self-service (desktop and mobile), the GOV.UK app (status checks and renewal reminders), telephone renewal via DVLA contact centre, and Post Office counter service (photo and identity verification). The service involves: identity verification, photo upload/capture, medical declarations, payment, and licence production. Currently 70% of renewals are online, 20% by phone, and 10% at Post Office counters. Design the domain layer, BFF structure, and explain how you ensure consistency across channels.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Consider which steps of the renewal journey are channel-specific (photo capture differs between online and Post Office) versus channel-agnostic (eligibility check, payment processing). Think about how the Post Office counter integrates — they verify identity in person but the transaction still needs to reach DVLA systems. Consider the GOV.UK app integration for proactive renewal reminders.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Multi-Channel Architecture: Driving Licence Renewal Service**

**Domain Layer (channel-agnostic):**
- Identity Verification Service: validates identity claims against existing DVLA records. Accepts verified identity assertions from any channel (GOV.UK One Login for web, agent verification for phone, in-person verification from Post Office).
- Eligibility Service: checks renewal eligibility (not disqualified, within renewal window, no outstanding medical declarations needed). Same rules regardless of channel.
- Medical Declaration Service: records medical self-declarations, flags for DVLA medical team review if triggers met.
- Photo Service: accepts photos from any source (upload, webcam, Post Office camera), validates against DVLA photo standards (biometric checks), stores approved photos.
- Payment Service: processes payment via GOV.UK Pay (web), card-over-phone (contact centre), or cash/card (Post Office via their payment integration).
- Licence Production Service: triggers licence production once all steps complete — same physical licence regardless of application channel.
- Notification Service: sends confirmation and tracking updates via citizen's preferred channel.

**BFF Layer:**

Citizen Web BFF:
- Progressive form journey: identity via GOV.UK One Login → eligibility check → photo upload (supports camera capture on mobile) → medical declarations → payment → confirmation
- Mobile-responsive — designed for phone-first given 60%+ mobile usage for this demographic
- Save-and-return: citizen can start on phone, finish on desktop

GOV.UK App BFF:
- Push notification when renewal is due (90 days, 30 days, 7 days before expiry)
- Licence status in document wallet (valid, expiring soon, expired)
- Deep link to renewal journey in web BFF or future in-app renewal flow
- Minimal data: licence status, expiry date, renewal eligibility

Contact Centre BFF:
- Agent verifies identity verbally (knowledge-based authentication) and records verification assertion
- Agent completes form on citizen's behalf: reads medical questions, records answers
- Photo: uses most recent valid photo on file (agent confirms with citizen) or arranges Post Office photo appointment
- Card payment taken over phone via PCI-compliant payment capture
- Agent can see renewal history and previous interactions across all channels

Post Office BFF:
- Post Office staff authenticate citizen with physical ID documents
- Photo captured in-branch using approved equipment, submitted via Post Office integration API
- Payment taken at counter, confirmation sent to DVLA via Post Office reconciliation feed
- Limited scope: Post Office handles identity + photo + payment only; medical declarations handled separately by DVLA

**Consistency Guarantees:**
- Eligibility rules exist only in Eligibility Service — one truth
- All channels produce the same renewal record in the same data store
- Caseworkers see a unified view regardless of submission channel
- Licence produced is identical regardless of application channel
- Photo standards enforced identically (automated biometric check runs regardless of photo source)

**Integration Points:**
- GOV.UK One Login: web channel identity
- Post Office Identity Service: in-person identity verification, photo capture
- GOV.UK Pay: web and phone payments
- GOV.UK Notify: email/SMS confirmations and reminders
- GOV.UK app: status and reminder integration via documented API

reflectiveQuestions: Think about a service you have worked on. Could a citizen get a different outcome depending on which channel they used? What architectural change would prevent that?
How does your service support users who start a transaction in one channel and need to continue in another (e.g., start online, get stuck, call the helpline)? Is context preserved across channels?
If your service added a new channel tomorrow (e.g., integration with the GOV.UK app), how much work would it require? Does your architecture make new channels easy or expensive?

Consider the contact centre agents for your service. Do they have purpose-built tools, or are they navigating the citizen-facing website on behalf of callers? What is the impact on call handling time and citizen experience?
How do you handle the 10% of users with very low digital skills? Is your architecture designed to support them, or does it assume everyone can self-serve digitally?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary architectural principle for multi-channel government services?
options: Build the web channel first and adapt it for other channels later
All business logic should reside in a channel-agnostic domain layer, with channels as thin presentation layers
Each channel should have its own independent implementation of business rules for maximum flexibility
Mobile channels should be deprioritised because government users prefer desktop
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The fundamental principle is separating what the service does (business logic in a shared domain layer) from how users interact with it (channel-specific presentation). This ensures consistent outcomes regardless of channel and means business rule changes are made once, not per-channel.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern provide in a multi-channel architecture?
options: A single shared backend that all channels use identically
A dedicated backend service per channel type that handles channel-specific concerns while delegating business logic to the domain layer
A frontend framework that automatically adapts to different devices
A caching layer that speeds up all channels equally
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The BFF pattern creates one backend per channel type (web BFF, agent BFF, mobile BFF, API BFF). Each handles channel-specific concerns like authentication, data shaping, and interaction patterns while calling shared domain services for business logic. This avoids one-size-fits-all backends that serve no channel well.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is 'assisted digital' architecturally significant?
options: It requires a completely separate system built for agents
It means the service must support agents completing transactions on behalf of citizens, requiring role-based access and audit trails through the same domain layer
It only applies to services used by elderly citizens
It is a design principle that has no architectural implications
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Assisted digital means agents, advisors, or carers complete transactions on behalf of citizens who cannot self-serve. Architecturally, this requires: the same domain layer (consistent outcomes), elevated access controls (agents can search citizens, override soft validations), audit trails (record who acted on behalf of whom), and purpose-built interfaces optimised for agent workflows.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main challenge of offline-first architecture for government services?
options: Offline-first is not possible with web technologies
Managing data synchronisation and conflict resolution when offline work must merge with server state
Government security requirements prohibit any local data storage
Users do not expect government services to work offline
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Offline-first architecture must handle what happens when locally-created data synchronises with the server — especially conflicts where both local and remote data have changed. Government services must define clear strategies (last-write-wins, merge, manual resolution) and communicate clearly to users what is available offline versus what requires connectivity.

knowledgeCheck.question: How should letter generation integrate with a multi-channel notification architecture?
options: Letters should be a completely separate system managed by a different team
Letters are another notification channel triggered by the same service events, using shared data but channel-appropriate templates
Letters should only be sent when the digital channel is unavailable
Letter content should be manually written by caseworkers for each recipient
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Letters are a notification channel like email or SMS. The same service events (decision made, deadline approaching) trigger letter generation using the same underlying data but formatted with letter-specific templates. This ensures consistency between what a citizen reads in an email and what they receive by post, and means letter content updates automatically when business rules change.
